items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Panmunjom armistice"?
options: The breakdown of relations between the PRC and the USSR from the late 1950s, leading to the withdrawal of Soviet advisers in 1960 and border clashes in 1969
US medium-range nuclear missiles based in Turkey and Italy, whose secret removal was part of the settlement of the crisis
The ceasefire signed on 27 July 1953 that ended fighting in Korea roughly along the 38th parallel without a peace treaty
The failed invasion of Cuba by CIA-trained Cuban exiles in April 1961
items.answer: The ceasefire signed on 27 July 1953 that ended fighting in Korea roughly along the 38th parallel without a peace treaty
items.markingKey: C. "Panmunjom armistice" is the ceasefire signed on 27 July 1953 that ended fighting in Korea roughly along the 38th parallel without a peace treaty.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Truman dismissed MacArthur in April 1951.
items.answer: MacArthur publicly called for attacks on China and the use of Nationalist troops, defying Truman’s policy of limited war and civilian control of the military.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: MacArthur publicly called for attacks on China and the use of Nationalist troops, defying Truman’s policy of limited war and civilian control of the military. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that the Korean War ended with a peace treaty in 1953. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It ended with an armistice signed at Panmunjom; no peace treaty has been signed and the two Koreas remain technically at war.
items.markingKey: It ended with an armistice signed at Panmunjom; no peace treaty has been signed and the two Koreas remain technically at war. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "The Korean War ended with a peace treaty in 1953." Explain why this is inaccurate.

Communism has passed beyond the use of subversion to conquer independent nations and will now use armed invasion and war. I have ordered United States air and sea forces to give the Korean government troops cover and support. I have ordered that the Seventh Fleet prevent any attack on Formosa.

What, according to Source B, were the main features of the Korean War (1950–1953)? [3]

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the Korean War was more important for its global consequences than for its effects on Korea.
items.answer: The war transformed the Cold War globally, but its human and political effects on Korea were profound and enduring.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: US rearmament and NSC-68; militarisation of NATO and West German rearmament; Sino-American hostility for two decades. Arguments against: millions of Korean dead and a lasting division; authoritarian regimes in both Koreas; refugees and separated families. Supported judgement: The war transformed the Cold War globally, but its human and political effects on Korea were profound and enduring.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The US National Security Council report of April 1950 recommending a massive military build-up to contain communism globally"?
items.answer: NSC-68
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of NSC-68.

items.stem: "The Korean War was solely a superpower proxy war." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It was also a Korean civil war over reunification, with Kim and Rhee both seeking to unify the peninsula.
items.markingKey: It was also a Korean civil war over reunification, with Kim and Rhee both seeking to unify the peninsula. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ExComm"?
options: The US belief, stated by Eisenhower in 1954, that if one country in a region fell to communism its neighbours would follow
The US naval blockade of Cuba announced by Kennedy on 22 October 1962 to stop further Soviet missiles reaching the island
The failed invasion of Cuba by CIA-trained Cuban exiles in April 1961
The Executive Committee of the National Security Council that advised Kennedy during the crisis
items.answer: The Executive Committee of the National Security Council that advised Kennedy during the crisis
items.markingKey: D. "ExComm" is the Executive Committee of the National Security Council that advised Kennedy during the crisis.

items.stem: Explain the difference between his second letter of 27 October and Khrushchev’s first letter of 26 October.
items.answer: The first letter offered to remove the missiles in return for a US pledge not to invade Cuba; the second, more formal letter added the demand that US Jupiter missiles be withdrawn from Turkey.

items.stem: Explain why the Cuban Missile Crisis led to improved superpower relations.
items.answer: Both leaders recognised how close they had come to nuclear war; the hotline was installed in 1963 and the Partial Test Ban Treaty was signed in August 1963.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961) and explain what it reveals about the causes of the Cuban Missile Crisis.
items.answer: About 1,400 CIA-trained exiles landed in Cuba and were defeated within three days; Kennedy refused air support. The invasion convinced Castro and Khrushchev that the USA would attack Cuba again, leading Castro to seek Soviet protection.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Khrushchev was the loser in the Cuban Missile Crisis."
items.answer: Khrushchev lost prestige, but he gained his main objectives; the outcome was closer to a compromise than a defeat.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: public withdrawal of missiles seemed humiliating; criticised by China and Castro; ousted in 1964 partly due to Cuba. Supported judgement: Khrushchev lost prestige, but he gained his main objectives; the outcome was closer to a compromise than a defeat.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that the Sino-Soviet split was caused more by national rivalry than by ideological differences.
items.answer: Ideological disputes expressed and intensified underlying national and personal rivalries.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: border disputes and the Ussuri clashes; Soviet refusal of nuclear technology; Mao’s desire to lead world communism. items.stem: Briefly explain why relations between China and the USSR broke down.
items.answer: Mao rejected de-Stalinisation and “peaceful coexistence”, resented Soviet refusal to share nuclear technology (1959) and saw himself as leader of world communism; Khrushchev criticised the Great Leap Forward; border disputes and rival national interests added to ideological conflict.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Chinese line on revolution and the Soviet line of peaceful coexistence.
items.answer: Khrushchev argued that communism could triumph through peaceful competition and avoid nuclear war; Mao insisted on continued revolutionary struggle, describing imperialism as a “paper tiger”.

items.stem: Distinguish between Khrushchev’s foreign policy and Stalin’s foreign policy.
items.answer: Stalin pursued caution combined with tight control of the Soviet bloc; Khrushchev promoted peaceful coexistence and engagement with the developing world but took greater risks in Berlin and Cuba.

items.stem: "Kennedy won the Cuban Missile Crisis without making any concessions." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Kennedy secretly agreed through Robert Kennedy to remove the Jupiter missiles from Turkey and publicly pledged not to invade Cuba.

items.stem: Distinguish between the war of stalemate (1951–53) and the war of movement (1950–51).
items.answer: In 1950–51 the front moved dramatically from the Pusan perimeter to the Yalu and back; from mid-1951 the front stabilised around the 38th parallel while armistice talks dragged on over the repatriation of prisoners.

items.stem: "Non-superpower states were merely puppets of the USA or USSR." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: States such as Cuba, China and North Vietnam often pursued their own aims and drew the superpowers into conflicts, such as Castro in Angola or Hanoi’s strategy in Vietnam.
